claims.claim: You don't need a faster language... A faster web language would speed up the part that doesn't matter
claims.about: Python web stack (Flask) vs faster-language web servers
claims.measured: python-flask 1,732 req/s plaintext vs go-gin 53,941, rust-actix 86,102, cpp-drogon 85,540 (1 CPU)
claims.why: The claim admits other languages serve web requests faster than Python, and the measurements agree: Flask is roughly 30–50x slower on raw throughput, which matters little at a few dozen jobs a day.

claims.claim: The web layer will do very little... At a few dozen runs a day it will be idle almost all the time
claims.measured: python-flask ~1,700 req/s plaintext, ~1,529 req/s single DB query on 1 CPU
claims.why: One Flask worker on one core handles about 1,500 requests per second, so a few dozen jobs a day (plus status polling) uses a tiny fraction of its capacity.

claims.claim: A 90-second run inside a request handler would tie up the web server
claims.about: Flask under Gunicorn with synchronous workers
claims.measured: python-flask I/O-wait test (10 ms per request): 276 req/s, p50 915 ms, 18% CPU; python-flask-gthread 374 req/s
claims.why: Even a 10 ms wait inside a handler cut sync Flask to 276 req/s with near-second latencies and an idle CPU, which shows blocked workers stall the server.

claims.claim: Rewriting in Go or Rust... would cost months and gain nothing measurable
claims.about: Go/Rust rewrite of the simulation or the service
claims.why: The cost sits in a NumPy simulation, and the benchmarks measure only web-server workloads, not NumPy against Go or Rust numerical code, so whether a rewrite would gain anything can't be checked.
